summary_findings: All three languages carry the Sanskrit twenty-seven in their own scripts and this file does not reproduce them: Biswas glosses each Bengali lemma 'the Nth of the twenty-seven zodiacal stars according to Hindu astronomy' (আর্দ্রা p. 126, অনুরাধা p. 36, অশ্লেষা p. 83), the Candrakanta Abhidhana does the same for Assamese (আৰ্দ্ৰা p. 102, ভৰণী p. 713), and Praharaj tabulates all twenty-seven with positions, star-counts, kaṭapayādi tags and Bayer letters in one enormous note under ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର (p. 4095) — where, incidentally, the Odia list heads the second asterism ଦ୍ୱିଜା Dwijā rather than Bharaṇī. What is not Sanskrit is what this file is for. THE PRIZE HOLDS AND IS BIGGER THAN EXPECTED: কালপুরুষ / কালপুৰুষ / କାଳପୁରୁଷ Kālapuruṣa for Orion is common to all three languages and has no Sanskrit ancestor as a constellation — in Sanskrit the word is Yama's black-bodied messenger and the jyotiṣa 'zodiac-man'. Biswas (p. 231) gives the Yama sense and the Orion sense side by side; Jñānendramohana Dāsa (p. 512) supplies the decisive gloss, parsing kāla as Yama in the etymology and as TIME in the astronomy — 'the star-cluster by which kāla, that is the rains and the other seasons, is measured' — and adds the alternate name অগ্রহায়ণী; Praharaj (p. 1552) keeps the 'black bodied' of the gloss, gives the same alternate name, and at p. 4095 numbers twenty-one stars of the figure, naming the belt Uṣā, Aniruddha and Citralekhā, the sword Mayūratuṇḍa and Rigel Bāṇarāja, so that in Odia the Kālapuruṣa figure is the frame the nakṣatras of that quarter of the sky are described BY (Ārdrā is 'the knob of Kālapuruṣa's right shoulder'). Both Dāsa and the Assamese dictionary count the figure as seven bright stars. Assamese adds a sky-figure of its own, গোধিকা godhikā, a northern chain shaped like a monitor lizard with the pole star at its tail-tip, attested from Śaṅkaradeva's Kīrttana — described as the Śiśumāra but glossed 'Big Bear', an inconsistency recorded and graded disputed. THE SECOND FINDING IS A SET OF ISOGLOSSES. The Milky Way is a ROAD everywhere in this region and only the traveller changes: an elephant-track in Assamese (হাতীপটি, Candrakanta p. 908) and Odia (ହାତିଦଣ୍ଡା, Praharaj p. 4095; Sambalpuri ହାଁଥିଧରସା p. 9036), both with the literal jungle sense standing as sense 1 of the same lemma; Yama's causeway in Bengali (যমের জাঙ্গাল / যমজাঙ্গাল, in Dāsa pp. 812 and 1811 and in both of Biswas's dictionaries); a cattle-track in Mundari (gaikoạ hora) and Kurukh (gā'e caur binkō). Bengali also has দুধপথ 'milk-road', which may be a calque. A comet is a BROOM in Bengali (ঝাঁটাতারা, marked গ্রাম্য by Dāsa, 'because it is shaped like a broom', p. 882; and Lal Behari Day's villagers call it 'a fiery broomstick') and in Mundari (jonọ ipil), and a TAIL in Odia (ଲଞ୍ଜା ତାରା), Assamese (নেজাল তৰা, attested by Bronson in 1867) and Kurukh (jhal binkō). ODIA IS THE RICHEST OF THE THREE, and its richest field is Venus, which has at least eight names split by apparition and by district — morning ଖଚୁଆ ତରା khacuā tarā ('the star that goes ahead to Yama and reports on the people of this world'), ଫୁକିଆ phukiā of the Garjat states ('when Phukiā rises the fisherwomen begin husking chuṛā'), କୁଆତରା kuātarā < kāvya-tārā, ପୁଆଁ ତରା and ପାହାନ୍ତି ତାରା; evening ପହରିକିଆ ତାରା and Sambalpuri କେଉଁଟି ତାରା, the fisher-caste star — and Praharaj is careful that 'morning star' names a function, not a body, since Mars, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn all fill the role (p. 4814). Bengali splits it শুকতারা / সাঁঝের তারা and Assamese পুবঁতী তৰা / ভোটাতৰা. Beneath standard Odia lies a Sambalpuri folk layer that Praharaj marks ପ୍ରାଦେ., and THIS LAYER IS ONLY INTELLIGIBLE AGAINST THE MUNDA AND DRAVIDIAN LANGUAGES AROUND IT (entered in the sibling file sources/tribal.json; cited here in the notes): the Pleiades are କଠଲା ତାରା 'the carpenter's mallet' in Sambalpuri and moṅgaru ipilko 'the wooden mallet the ploughman flung at the dove' in Mundari; the Big Dipper is ବାଜ୍ଖଟ୍ 'the corpse-bier' in Sambalpuri, topa gaṛa parkom ipilko 'the bier stars' in Mundari and khaṭī pawā bīnkō in Kurukh; Orion's Belt is ନଙ୍ଗଲ ଜୁଡ଼ା 'the yoked plough' in Sambalpuri — with the note that the Khaṛiās will not yoke the plough or sow paddy until it has risen, i.e. not before Baiśākha (p. 4106) — and arar 'the Yoke' in Santali, araṛ ipilko in Mundari, ugtā pagsi binkō in Kurukh. The three Sambalpuri names are not curiosities; they are the Odia end of Munda figures, and that is the single most useful thing this pass established about Odia. Standard Odia meanwhile calls the Big Dipper ସାତଭାଇୟା 'the seven brothers' and the Pleiades କାର୍ତ୍ତିକପୁଞ୍ଜ, marked deśī and carrying a proverb. NEGATIVE FINDINGS, which are half the result. The agricultural-calendar material the brief expected from the gazetteer literature IS NOT THERE: all twenty volumes of Hunter's Statistical Account of Bengal and both of the Statistical Account of Assam were downloaded and grepped and yield exactly one astronomical sentence between them, a quotation of Dalton on the ṛṣis of the Great Bear; the District Gazetteers of Sambalpur, Puri, Cuttack, Balasore, Angul, Santal Parganas, Ranchi, Kamrup, Darrang, Nowgong, Sibsagar and Goalpara yield nothing; the Census reports of 1901 and 1911 yield nothing; Dalton 1872 and Risley 1891 yield only the Santal sept-name and two Sanskrit remarks. The one agricultural marker in this file comes from a DICTIONARY, not a gazetteer. Arcturus and Antares have no vernacular name in any of the three languages — 'Arcturus' returns nothing at all in Biswas or Praharaj, and Antares appears only as an English label inside Praharaj's Jyeṣṭhā table. Bengali and Assamese have the Orion figure but no name for its waist: no Bengali word for Orion's Belt was found in any source, and Dāsa describes it in English without naming it. No pre-1900 attestation of কালপুরুষ = Orion was reached: Haughton 1833 and Ram Comul Sen 1834 do not have it, and Sen renders the English headword Orion descriptively as দক্ষিণদিকস্থ রাশিবিশেষ, তারাবিশেষ 'a certain sign in the southern sky, a certain star'; the earliest attestation here is Dāsa's second edition of 1937, with the Assamese and Odia dictionaries following. Bengali proved the thinnest of the three for folk material: outside কালপুরুষ, ঝাঁটাতারা, পোয়াতে-তারা, তারা খসা and যমের জাঙ্গাল its astronomical vocabulary is almost entirely tatsama. Two words were chased and dropped: the Ḍākabacana couplet Praharaj prints under the Orion word ଅଦ୍ରାବଳି turns out from his own entries at pp. 813-814 and 1080 to be about RAINBOWS east and west, not Orion, so it is not evidence of an Odia agricultural asterism; and Bronson's Assamese-English dictionary of 1867, though it proved to hold the best-dated words in the file, is unusable by grep — the archive.org OCR of its Assamese fount is noise, and its four astronomical entries had to be read off the page images one at a time.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the man of Kāla' — Kāla being both Time and Death (Yama); hence 'the Time-man / the black man', Yama's envoy
entries.usage_note: The ordinary modern Bengali word for Orion; it is the name under which the figure is taught in Bengali schoolbooks and popular astronomy, and it has no counterpart in the Sanskrit star-lists, where Orion is Mṛga/Prajāpati and only its parts (Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Iṣus trikāṇḍā) are named.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. কালপুরুষ kālapuruṣa, p. 231
entries.quote: কালপুরুষ kālapuruṣa n. (myth.) an attendant or envoy of Yama, the god of death; (astr.) the Orion.
entries.notes: This is the flagship entry for this database: a constellation figure named in the modern eastern NIA languages and not inherited as a constellation name from Sanskrit. In Sanskrit, kālapuruṣa is (a) Yama's black-bodied messenger and (b) in jyotiṣa the 'zodiacal man' on whose body the twelve rāśis are laid out; neither is the constellation Orion. The transfer of the name to Orion is shared by Bengali, Odia and Assamese (see the Odia and Assamese entries here) and is therefore an eastern-Indian innovation, not a Bengali one alone. Praharaj's Odia entry preserves the 'black-bodied' gloss that Biswas's English shortens to 'attendant or envoy of Yama'.

entries.literal_meaning: 'Śukra-star' — a worn-down compound of Śukra (Venus) + tārā (star)
entries.usage_note: Biswas glosses it 'the vesper', i.e. the EVENING star, although in ordinary Bengali speech শুকতারা is most often the MORNING star and সন্ধ্যাতারা the evening one. Praharaj, listing Bengali equivalents for his Odia headwords, prints শুকতারা against BOTH ପାହାନ୍ତି ତାରା (morning) and ପହରିକିଆ ତାରା (evening). The divergence is real and old; the underlying object is the same planet.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. শুকতারা śukatārā, p. 950
entries.quote: শুকতারা śukatārā n. the vesper; (astr.) Venus.
entries.notes: Contrast the tatsama শুক্র śukra at the same page, glossed '(astr.) the Venus; the vesper'. শুকতারা is the tadbhava household form.

entries.usage_note: Sub-lemma ~তারা under the headword সন্ধ্যা. The learned doublet সান্ধ্যতারা / সান্ধ্যতারকা is at p. 1005.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. সন্ধ্যা sandhyā, sub-lemma ~তারা, p. 979
entries.quote: ~তারা n. the evening star, the Vesper.

entries.literal_meaning: 'Yama's jāṅgāl' — a jāṅgāl is a raised earthen causeway or embankment across flooded land
entries.usage_note: Sub-lemma ~জাঙ্গাল under the headword যম (Yama, god of death). The image is of the galaxy as the raised road on which the dead travel — the deltaic-Bengal counterpart of the Odia hātidaṇḍā and Assamese hātīpaṭi 'elephant-track' (both in this file).
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. যম yama (2), sub-lemma ~জাঙ্গাল, p. 890
entries.quote: ~জাঙ্গাল n. the Milky Way, the Galaxy.
entries.notes: জাঙ্গাল is a Bengali (not Sanskrit) word for an embankment/raised road; the compound is therefore formed in Bengali even though its first member is the Sanskrit theonym. Note the Bengali word for the Milky Way that everyone knows, ছায়াপথ, is a separate sanskritic entry here.

entries.usage_note: The ordinary modern Bengali word for the galaxy, and the one used in Bengali popular science.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ছায়া chāẏā, sub-lemma ~পথ, p. 379
entries.quote: ~পথ n. galaxy, the Milky Way.

entries.usage_note: Marked '(rare)'. This is a semantic shift, not an inheritance: in the Sanskrit sources Ajavīthī is one of the nine vīthīs, a three-nakṣatra segment of the ecliptic belt (see sanskrit_db_id ajavithi), never the galaxy. Both Biswas for Bengali and the Chandrakanta Abhidhana for Assamese gloss it 'Milky Way', so the shift is shared across the eastern lexicographic tradition.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. অজবীথি ajabīthi, p. 12
entries.quote: অজবীথি ajabīthi n. (rare) a chariot for gods; the Milky Way, the Galaxy.
entries.notes: Flagged disputed because the identification is the lexicographers', and it contradicts the Sanskrit astronomical meaning of the word. The Assamese entry (Chandrakanta p. 10) keeps BOTH readings side by side: it glosses ajabīthi as হাতীপটি / ছায়াপথ 'milky way' and then, in the Assamese definition, correctly describes it as one of the three roads of the sun, moon and planets containing Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā.

entries.usage_note: The Sanskrit star-name surviving unaltered in the modern Bengali lexicon, with its hunter etymology still transparent in the same entry.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. লুব্ধ lubdha, sub-entry লুব্ধক, p. 930
entries.quote: লুব্ধক n. a hunter; a fowler; a lecher; (astr.) the Sirius, the Dogstar.

entries.usage_note: The entry carries into modern Bengali the Agastya-yātrā observance keyed to the star's heliacal rising in Bhādra.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. অগস্ত্য agastya, p. 6
entries.quote: অগস্ত্য agastya n. a mythological sage of India; (astrol.) the Canopus. ~যাত্রা n. the first day of the month of Bhadra (ভাদ্র) when the sage Agastya asked the bending Vindhyas to wait till he came back and he never came back (this day has since been regarded by the Hindus as extremely inauspicious to set out on a journey…)

entries.usage_note: Bengali keeps the old Vedic ṛkṣa 'bear ~ star' ambiguity live in a single dictionary entry: the headword is glossed 'the bear; a star; a constellation', and the compound is the Great Bear.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ঋক্ষ r̥kṣa, sub-lemma ~মণ্ডল, p. 176
entries.quote: ঋক্ষ r̥kṣa n. (for. the bear; a star; a constellation. ~মণ্ডল n. (astr.) The Saptarshi, the Great Bear. ~রাজ, ঋক্ষেশ n. the moon (when personified).
entries.notes: '(for.' in the printed text is a truncated bracket in the DSAL transcription; the sense is unaffected.

entries.usage_note: Biswas is the source that shows the modern Bengali equation of the group with the English 'Plough' as well as the Great Bear.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. সপ্ত sapta, sub-lemma ~র্ষি, p. 981
entries.quote: ~র্ষি n. the seven great ancient sages of India; (astr.) the Plough; (astr.) the Great Bear, the Ursa Major (also সপ্তর্ষিমন্ডল).

entries.usage_note: The entry keeps both the Purāṇic prince and the star in one lemma, and the adjectival sense 'sure, certain, fixed' alongside them.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ধ্রুব dhruba, p. 548
entries.quote: ধ্রুব dhruba n. (myth.) a prince famous for his incomparable devotion to God Hari (হরি); the Pole Star, the Polaris, the North Star, the cynosure, ☐ a. sure, certain; fixed; firm, deep-seated (ধ্রুববিশ্বাস); constant; actual, real (ধ্রুব সত্য).

entries.usage_note: Sub-lemmas under তারা. The learned word উল্কা ulkā is at p. 172 ('an aerolite or aerolith, a shooting star, a meteor'); তারাপতন is the transparent Bengali compound beside it.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. তারা tārā, sub-lemmas ~পতন, ~পাত, p. 458
entries.quote: ~পতন, ~পাত n. the fall of a meteor. ~পথ n. the stellar course; the sky, the welkin. … ~মণ্ডল n. the stellar region or orbit; a constellation.

entries.usage_note: Beside the ordinary ধূমকেতু dhūmaketu (p. 544). The comet as a decapitated body is the same figure as the Rāhu/Ketu myth, and Biswas's entry runs the three senses together.
entries.citation: Sailendra Biswas, Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed., Calcutta: Sahitya Samsad, 2000 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. কবন্ধ kabandha, p. 202
entries.quote: কবন্ধ kabandha n. a headless or truncated body; a headless or truncated goblin; the ascending node, the descending node; a comet.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the broom star' — Dāsa's own bracket says 'because it is shaped like a broom'
entries.usage_note: The Bengali folk comet-word, standing beside the learned ধূমকেতু, whose definition in the same dictionary (p. 1147) also reaches for the broom: 'a luminous body whose rays are shaped like a jhāṛu'.
entries.citation: Jñānendramohana Dāsa, Bāṅgālā Bhāṣāra Abhidhāna, 2nd rev. ed., Kalikātā: Indian Publishing House [bhūmikā 1937] (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ঝাঁটাতারা jhām̐ṭātārā, p. 882
entries.quote: ঝাঁটাতারা jhām̐ṭātārā [গ্রা◦। ঝাঁটার আকার বলিয়া] বি, ধুমকেতু।
entries.notes: Register folk on the dictionary's own authority: গ্রা◦ = গ্রাম্য, rustic/colloquial. Compare the eastern 'tail-star' words — Assamese নেজাল তৰা, Odia ଲଞ୍ଜା ତାରା / ଲାଙ୍ଗୁଡ଼ା ତାରା — all in this file. Bengali has reached for a different household object. Corroborated from outside lexicography: Lal Behari Day, Bengal Peasant Life, ch. VIII 'The Village Astrologer', p. 61 (ed. of 1916), reports a village astrologer's reputation made by predicting famine and pestilence "from the appearance in the heavens of a 'fiery broomstick,' as the people called the comet" — the English of the same figure, with no Bengali form printed. And the Mundas of Chota Nagpur call a comet jonọ ipil, the broom star (this file).

entries.literal_meaning: 'the dawning star' — Dāsa derives it from প্রভাতিয়া prabhātiyā, 'of the dawn'
entries.usage_note: Illustrated from a work Dāsa abbreviates গ্রহ-নক্ষত্র ('Planets and Stars'): 'have you seen the poẏāte-tārā, or śuk-tārā?' — the citation itself glossing the folk word with the standard one.
entries.citation: Jñānendramohana Dāsa, Bāṅgālā Bhāṣāra Abhidhāna, 2nd rev. ed., Kalikātā: Indian Publishing House [bhūmikā 1937] (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. পোয়াতে-তারা poẏāte-tārā, p. 1386
entries.quote: পোয়াতে-তারা poẏāte-tārā [প্রভাতিয়া >] বি, শুকতারা। "তোমরা পা◦ তা◦ বা শুক তারাকে দেখিয়াছ কি?"-গ্রহ-নক্ষত্র।
entries.notes: This is the Bengali member of the eastern 'dawn-star' set: Assamese পুবঁতী তৰা, Odia ପାହାନ୍ତି ତାରା and ପୁଆଁ ତରା (the last also from প্রভাতী তারা). All four are independent worn-down reflexes of a 'dawn' word plus 'star'. DSAL's headword index encodes this lemma's য় as U+09DF.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the star of dusk' (sāñjh, the colloquial Bengali for evening)
entries.usage_note: Given by Dāsa as the plain Bengali equivalent of the learned সান্ধ্যতারা, alongside শুক্রতারা.
entries.citation: Jñānendramohana Dāsa, Bāṅgālā Bhāṣāra Abhidhāna, 2nd rev. ed., Kalikātā: Indian Publishing House [bhūmikā 1937] (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. সান্ধ্য sāndhya, sub-lemma ̃তারা, p. 2046
entries.quote: সান্ধ্য sāndhya [সন্ধ্যা + অ (ভবার্থে)] বিণ, সায়ংকালীন। 2 সন্ধ্যাসম্বন্ধীয়। ̃তারা -সাঁঝের তারা; শুক্রতারা evening star; vesper.

entries.usage_note: Listed by Dāsa among the Bengali synonyms of ছায়াপথ, and again under হরিতালী (p. 2133). This is the one indigenous eastern name for the galaxy that agrees with the European one, and Dāsa gives it without comment beside আকাশগঙ্গা and যমের জাঙ্গাল.
entries.citation: Jñānendramohana Dāsa, Bāṅgālā Bhāṣāra Abhidhāna, 2nd rev. ed., Kalikātā: Indian Publishing House [bhūmikā 1937] (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ছায়া chāẏā, sub-lemma ̃পথ, p. 812
entries.quote: ̃পথ [ছায়া (জ্যোতিঃ) পথ (পথ সদৃশ বলিয়া] বি, জ্যোতিশ্চক্রের মধ্যস্হিত পথের ন্যায় দৃশ্যমান অর্দ্ধমণ্ডলাকার নক্ষত্রপুঞ্জ; আকাশগঙ্গা; দুধপথ; যমের জাঙ্গাল।
entries.notes: Whether দুধপথ is a nineteenth-century calque on 'Milky Way' or older is not settled by this entry; Dāsa gives no etymology and no citation for it. It is absent from Biswas. Treat as possibly a translation.

entries.usage_note: The second, independent attestation of the name — Dāsa lists it among the synonyms of ছায়াপথ (p. 812) and again as a sub-headword under যম (p. 1811), where it is equated with আকাশগঙ্গা, সোমধারা, দেবপথ and ছায়াপথ.
entries.citation: Jñānendramohana Dāsa, Bāṅgālā Bhāṣāra Abhidhāna, 2nd rev. ed., Kalikātā: Indian Publishing House [bhūmikā 1937] (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. যম yama, sub-lemma ̃জাঙ্গাল, p. 1811
entries.quote: ̃জাঙ্গাল -বি, আকাশগঙ্গা; নভোমণ্ডলস্হিত সোমধারা; দেবপথ বা ছায়াপথ the milky way.
entries.notes: Three independent Bengali dictionaries carry it: Dāsa here and at p. 812, Biswas's Samsad Bengali-English at p. 890 (যমজাঙ্গাল), and Biswas's Bengali-Bengali Saṃsada Bāṅgālā Abhidhāna, 7th ed. 2004, p. 305, which lists 'আকাশগঙ্গা, যমের জাঙ্গাল, milky way' under ছায়াপথ. The genitive form যমের জাঙ্গাল is the spoken one.

entries.literal_meaning: uncertain; the word's other senses are the bright-fourth of Bhādra and dūrvā grass
entries.usage_note: Defined by its orientation: 'a white line running north-and-south across the path of the sky'. Praharaj's Odia entries for the same word (pp. 8972-8973) define it the same way and with the same orientation clause, and list it among the Sanskrit names of the Chāyāpatha at p. 4095.
entries.citation: Jñānendramohana Dāsa, Bāṅgālā Bhāṣāra Abhidhāna, 2nd rev. ed., Kalikātā: Indian Publishing House [bhūmikā 1937] (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. হরিতালী, হরিতালিকা haritālī, haritālikā, p. 2133
entries.quote: হ̑রিতালী, হ̑রিতালিকা haritālī, haritālikā [সং] বি, আকাশমার্গে উত্তরদক্ষিণব্যাপী শ্বেত রেখা; ছায়াপথ; আকাশগঙ্গা; দুধপথ the milky-way.
entries.notes: A real cross-language link: Bengali and Odia lexicography independently carry Haritālī as a Milky Way word with an orientation clause, and neither cites a Sanskrit source. Both mark it সং./ସଂ. I have found it in no Sanskrit lexicon, so sanskrit_db_id is null and confidence is likely, not certain. Dāsa's ̑ marks are his own vowel-length diacritics, reproduced as DSAL prints them.

entries.literal_meaning: Dāsa parses it 'Kāla (= Yama), his puruṣa (= assistant)', a genitive tatpuruṣa; but his second sense reads Kāla as TIME — 'the star-cluster that measures kāla, i.e. the rains and the other seasons'
entries.usage_note: The second and better Bengali source for the prize word. Dāsa gives the alternative name অগ্রহায়ণী Agrahāyaṇī, and appends an English note describing the belt: 'one of the constellations containing seven very bright stars, three of which in a straight line, form Orion's belt'.
entries.citation: Jñānendramohana Dāsa, Bāṅgālā Bhāṣāra Abhidhāna, 2nd rev. ed., Kalikātā: Indian Publishing House [bhūmikā 1937] (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. কালপুরুষ kālapuruṣa, p. 512
entries.quote: কালপুরুষ kālapuruṣa [কাল (যম) তার পুরুষ (সহকারী)-6 তৎ] বি, যমকিঙ্কর; যমের ভৃত্য। 2 পুরুষাকৃতি নক্ষত্রপুঞ্জ; কাল- (বর্ষাদি ঋতু) পরিমাপক নক্ষত্রপুঞ্জ; ইহার নামান্তর অগ্রহায়ণী the constellation Orion […] 3 শুভাশুভ জ্ঞাতার্থে জন্মলগ্নাদি কল্পিত দ্বাদশ রাশি।
entries.notes: This entry settles the 'Time-man' question: Bengali lexicography itself reads kāla BOTH ways, as Death in the etymology and as season-time in the astronomical sense — 'the cluster by which the seasons are measured'. The seven-bright-star count in the English note is the same reckoning the Assamese dictionary gives (Candrakanta p. 210), and the alternative name Agrahāyaṇī is the same one Praharaj gives for Odia (p. 1552). The three dictionaries are describing one eastern tradition.

entries.usage_note: Dāsa defines the Sanskrit উল্কাপাত by this ordinary Bengali phrase and by nothing else.
entries.citation: Jñānendramohana Dāsa, Bāṅgālā Bhāṣāra Abhidhāna, 2nd rev. ed., Kalikātā: Indian Publishing House [bhūmikā 1937] (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. উল্কা ulkā, sub-lemma ̃পাত, p. 349
entries.quote: ̃পাত -বি, তারা খসা। ̃পিণ্ড-বি, উল্কাশ্ম meteor.
entries.notes: খসা is the verb used of a thing coming unfastened and slipping down; the same verb is used of a miscarriage (গা খসা). Bengali has no 'falling' in the phrase, only 'coming loose'.

entries.region: Bengal (stated by the dictionary to be the usage of 'this country')
entries.usage_note: Recorded because of the explicit statement of regional usage in the parenthesis: 'in this country a meteor-fall is called nakṣatrapāta'. The same entry supplies the colloquial Bengali pronunciations of নক্ষত্র — নোক্খোত্তোর, নখতর, নোখতা.
entries.citation: Jñānendramohana Dāsa, Bāṅgālā Bhāṣāra Abhidhāna, 2nd rev. ed., Kalikātā: Indian Publishing House [bhūmikā 1937] (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. নক্ষত্র nakṣatra, sub-lemma ̃পাত, p. 1157
entries.quote: ̃পাত [নক্ষত্র-পাত (পতন), 6তৎ] ক্রি-বি, ভূতলে নক্ষত্রের পতন (এ দেশে উল্কাপাতকে নক্ষত্রপাত বলে)। 2 [কাব্যা- লঙ্কারে] নক্ষত্রের আকাশ হতে পতনের ন্যায় উচ্চপদ হতে মানী ব্যক্তির অধঃপতন; মহাত্মার দেহপাত।
entries.notes: The second sense is a figure of speech in living use — the death of a great man, illustrated from what the newspapers wrote on Keshab Chandra Sen's death: 'today a star has fallen'.

modern_star.common_name: Meissa and the head of Orion

entries.literal_meaning: Ilvala, the asura brother of Vātāpi
entries.usage_note: Haughton marks both as feminine and 'used in the plural only' — the Vedic plural Ilvalāḥ preserved intact in a Bengali dictionary of 1833.
entries.citation: Sir Graves Champney Haughton, A Dictionary, Bengáli and Sanskrit, explained in English, London: printed by J. L. Cox and Son, 1833, s.v. ইলবকা / ইলবলা, p. 419
entries.quote: ইলবকা s. (f. used in the plural only) Stars in the head of Orion. See ইলবলা. — ইলবলা s. (f. used in the plural only) Stars in the head of Orion.
entries.notes: THE POINT OF THIS ENTRY IS THE CONTRAST. Bengali keeps Ilvalā where Sanskrit had it, on Orion's HEAD (compare the Sanskrit database entry ilvala, from the Taittirīya tradition). Odia has moved the same word down to Orion's BELT — Praharaj s.v. ଇଲ୍ୱଳା p. 876, and again at pp. 1552 and 4106. Two neighbouring languages, one inherited word, two different asterisms. Transcribed from the page image, which I read directly: Haughton's fount cuts র as ৰ throughout, and the headwords are printed with plain ব, ইলবকা / ইলবলা, not the conjunct ল্ব of the Odia form.

entries.sky_object: the Pleiades — as glossed by an 1834 English-Bengali dictionary
entries.usage_note: Recorded as a divergence, not as a name to be used. Ram Comul Sen renders the English headword Pleiades by সপ্তর্ষি, which in every other source in this file — Bengali, Assamese and Odia alike — is Ursa Major.
entries.citation: Ram Comul Sen, A Dictionary in English and Bengalee, vol. 2, Serampore, 1834, s.v. Pleiades, p. 168
entries.quote: Pleiades বা Pleiads, n. s. Lat. Gr. সপ্তর্ষি।
entries.notes: Read directly from the page image. The error is worth keeping for the same reason as the Assamese অৰুন্ধতী entry: it is a recurring one, and it has a cause. Both the Pleiades and the Big Dipper are seven-star groups, and Purāṇic myth ties them — six of the seven ṛṣis' wives were driven from their husbands' sides and became the Kṛttikās (Praharaj p. 4095). A lexicographer reaching for 'the seven' can land on either. The correct Bengali is কৃত্তিকা, which Mendies's Companion to Johnson's Dictionary (1876) glosses simply 'the Pleiades; Karttika's nurse'.

entries.usage_note: Assamese has the same Orion-figure as Bengali and Odia. What is distinctively Assamese is the reckoning: the dictionary defines the figure as 'the group containing seven very bright stars' (সাতোটা অতি উজ্জ্বল নক্ষত্ৰ থকা ৰাশি), i.e. Orion counted as seven bright stars rather than by its parts.
entries.citation: Candrakanta Abhidhana (Assamese-Assamese-English), 2nd ed., Guwahati: Guwahati Bisbabidyalaya for the Assam Sahitya Sabha, 1962 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. কালপুৰুষ kālapuruṣa, p. 210
entries.quote: কালপুৰুষ kālapuruṣa বি. সুৰুতি ব্ৰহ্মৰ্ষিৰ ভেশ ধৰি ৰামচন্দ্ৰক স্বৰ্গলৈ নিবলৈ অহা এজন পুৰুষৰ নাম … 2। সাতোটা অতি উজ্জ্বল নক্ষত্ৰ থকা ৰাশি; the constellation Orion. 3। মৱত্যু-দেবতা।
entries.notes: The DSAL transcription of this dictionary renders the Assamese vowel sign ৃ as ৱ throughout (মৱত্যু for মৃত্যু, কৱত্তিকা for কৃত্তিকা). The headword কালপুৰুষ itself is unaffected. In sense 1 the Assamese tradition additionally identifies Kālapuruṣa as the figure who came in the guise of the brahmarṣi Suruti to take Rāmacandra to heaven — a Rāmāyaṇa episode, not the Yama-messenger of the Bengali and Odia dictionaries.

entries.literal_meaning: 'elephant-track' — the beaten path elephants make through jungle
entries.usage_note: The primary sense in the dictionary is the literal jungle elephant-track; the galaxy is sense 2. Exactly the same metaphor, with the same primary sense, is the recorded Odia name — ହାତିଦଣ୍ଡା hātidaṇḍā (Praharaj p. 4095, and Sambalpuri ହାଁଥିଧରସା p. 9036). This is the strongest vernacular isogloss in this file.
entries.citation: Candrakanta Abhidhana (Assamese-Assamese-English), 2nd ed., Guwahati: Guwahati Bisbabidyalaya for the Assam Sahitya Sabha, 1962 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. হাতীপটি hātīpaṭi, p. 908
entries.quote: হাতীপটি hātīpaṭi বি. হাৰিৰ মাজৰ হাতীয়ে চলাচল কৰা বাট; a track of elephant in jungle. 2। আকাশত ওলোবা সৰু সৰু তৰাৰ শাৰী; অজৰীথি; the milky way.
entries.notes: 'হাৰিৰ' and 'অজৰীথি' in the DSAL text are OCR for হাবিৰ (jungle) and অজবীথি; the entry cross-refers to the অজবীথি lemma at p. 10, which is glossed 'হাতীপটি; ছায়াপথ; milky-way'.

entries.sky_object: a lizard-shaped circumpolar star figure with the Pole Star at its tail-tip

modern_star.common_name: circumpolar figure — glossed 'the Big Bear' but described as a lizard-shaped chain ending at Polaris

entries.usage_note: A genuine Assamese sky-figure, and an old one: the dictionary supports it with a line from the Kīrttana (the Kīrttana-ghoṣā of Śaṅkaradeva, 16th c.) — 'গোধিকাৰ পুছ ভাগে দেখিয় অদ্যাপি', 'even today it is seen at the tail-end of the Godhikā'.
entries.citation: Candrakanta Abhidhana (Assamese-Assamese-English), 2nd ed., Guwahati: Guwahati Bisbabidyalaya for the Assam Sahitya Sabha, 1962 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. গোধিকা godhikā, p. 308
entries.quote: গোধিকা godhikā [সং.] বি. গুঁই; the iguana. 2। আকাশৰ উত্তৰ ফালে গুঁইৰ আকৱতিৰ নিচিনা হৈ শাৰী পাতি থকা কেতেবোৰ তৰা [তাৰ নেজৰ মূৰত ধ্ৰুব তৰা আছে।]; যেনে-"গোধিকাৰ পুছ ভাগে দেখিয় অদ্যাপি" (কীৰ্ত্তন); a number of stars in the north forming the figure of an iguana at the tail of which is situated the pole star; the "Big Bear" constellation.
entries.notes: The identification is internally inconsistent and I have graded it accordingly. The Assamese description — a row of stars in the north shaped like a monitor lizard, WITH DHRUVA AT THE TIP OF ITS TAIL — is the Purāṇic Śiśumāra, the circumpolar porpoise/reptile figure whose tail-tip is the pole star (Ursa Minor with Draco), not Ursa Major, whose stars are nowhere near the pole. The dictionary's own English gloss nevertheless says 'the Big Bear constellation'. I record the Assamese as printed and reject the English equation. Linked to shishumara on that reasoning; 'আকৱতিৰ' is DSAL OCR for আকৃতিৰ.

entries.usage_note: Glossed by the tatsama ধূমকেতু. The same 'tail-star' formation is the ordinary Odia word (ଲଞ୍ଜା ତାରା lañjā tārā, ଲାଙ୍ଗୁଡ଼ା ତାରା lāṅguṛā tārā, in this file); Praharaj's synonym column prints a Bengali cognate against it as well.
entries.citation: Candrakanta Abhidhana (Assamese-Assamese-English), 2nd ed., Guwahati: Guwahati Bisbabidyalaya for the Assam Sahitya Sabha, 1962 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. নেজাল তৰা nejāla tarā, p. 562
entries.quote: নেজাল তৰা nejāla, tarā বি. ধূমকেতু; এবিধ তৰা; a comet.
entries.notes: Attested in Assamese as early as 1867: Bronson, A Dictionary in Assamese and English, p. 327, 'নেজাল তৰা, s. নেজ লগা তৰা বিসেস, a comet' (separate entry in this file). The tail-star formation is pan-eastern — Odia ଲଞ୍ଜା ତାରା and ଲାଙ୍ଗୁଡ଼ା ତାରା, Kurukh jhal binkō. Hoffmann's guess that the tail-word for a comet was 'first coined by Missionaries' (Encyclopaedia Mundarica VII, p. 1923) cannot hold for Indo-Aryan given this 1867 attestation and the Odia poetic citation from Rādhānātha.

entries.usage_note: The everyday Assamese word: the dictionary's own definition of উল্কা ulkā (p. 140) ends by equating it with পপীয়া তৰা. A meteor is bad luck made visible, and the name says so.
entries.citation: Candrakanta Abhidhana (Assamese-Assamese-English), 2nd ed., Guwahati: Guwahati Bisbabidyalaya for the Assam Sahitya Sabha, 1962 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. পপীয়া papīẏā, sub-lemma পপীয়া-তৰা, p. 575
entries.quote: পপীয়া papīẏā [সং. পাপ] বিণ. পাপী; অধৰ্ম্মী; sinful. পপীয়া-তৰা বি. উল্কা; a meteor; a shooting-star.
entries.notes: The DSAL headword index encodes this lemma's য় with the precomposed BENGALI LETTER YYA (U+09DF); the source_url above uses that encoding, and a query typed with য + nukta returns nothing. The lemma is also absent from DSAL's page-level browse of p. 575. Also attested a century earlier, in the same spelling minus the long ī: Bronson (1867), p. 72, glosses উল্কাপাত with পপিয়া তৰা. Bronson's Assamese can only be read off the page images; the archive.org OCR of this dictionary's script is noise.

entries.literal_meaning: uncertain; 'the kukurabāhī stars' — most plausibly kukurā 'fowl' + bāhī 'nest, roost', i.e. a brood of stars, matching the second Assamese word for the same thing, থুপিতৰা 'clustered stars'
entries.usage_note: The living Assamese word for a star-cluster, and the word the dictionary itself uses to define সপ্তৰ্ষি-মণ্ডল at p. 859 ('একলগে থকা এজাক কুকুৰ-বাহী তৰা', 'a flock of kukurabāhī stars together'). Its synonym থুপিতৰা thupi-tarā is at p. 483.
entries.citation: Candrakanta Abhidhana (Assamese-Assamese-English), 2nd ed., Guwahati: Guwahati Bisbabidyalaya for the Assam Sahitya Sabha, 1962 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. কুকুৰবাহী তৰা kukurabāhī tarā, p. 216
entries.quote: কুকুৰবাহী তৰা kukurabāhī, tarā বি. খোপা বান্ধি ওচৰা-উচৰি হৈ-থকা সৰু সৰু তৰাৰ জাক বা জুম; থুপিতৰা; a constellation.
entries.notes: Confidence 'unidentified' refers to the sky object, not the word: the dictionary defines it generically, and does not tie it to any one cluster. I have deliberately NOT read it as the Pleiades, even though 'hen and chickens' is a standard European name for that cluster and Praharaj gives 'Hen and chickens' among the western names of Kṛttikā (p. 4095); the Assamese entry does not say so. The literal meaning is my reading of the compound and is marked as such.

entries.usage_note: Sense 7 of the polysemous headword মণ্ডল: 'the seven stars clustered near the sign Taurus'. Using the bare word maṇḍala, with no qualifier, for the Pleiades is an Assamese usage; Bengali and Odia both require a compound (কৃত্তিকা / କାର୍ତ୍ତିକପୁଞ୍ଜ).
entries.citation: Candrakanta Abhidhana (Assamese-Assamese-English), 2nd ed., Guwahati: Guwahati Bisbabidyalaya for the Assam Sahitya Sabha, 1962 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. মণ্ডল maṇḍala, sense 7, p. 735
entries.quote: 7। বৱষ ৰাশিৰ ওচৰত থোপা বান্ধি থকা সাতোটা তৰা; the Pleiades.
entries.notes: 'বৱষ' is DSAL OCR for বৃষ 'Taurus'. Graded 'likely' rather than 'certain' only because the sense is one of eight in a crowded entry and is not separately illustrated.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the dawn star' (pubā 'to dawn, to break — of night')
entries.usage_note: Given inside the entry for শুক্ৰ as the Assamese equivalent of the tatsama planet-name. This is the Assamese member of the eastern set of 'dawn-star' words for Venus — cf. Odia ପାହାନ୍ତି ତାରା pāhānti tārā and ପୁଆଁ ତରା puāñ tarā in this file.
entries.citation: Candrakanta Abhidhana (Assamese-Assamese-English), 2nd ed., Guwahati: Guwahati Bisbabidyalaya for the Assam Sahitya Sabha, 1962 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. শুক্ৰ śukra, p. 843
entries.quote: শুক্ৰ śukra [সং.] বি. ভৱগু মুনিৰ পুতেক-দৈত্য-গুৰু; the preceptor of the Asuras. 2। ছয় সংখ্যাৰ গ্ৰহৰ নাম; পুবঁতী- তৰা; Venus, the morning star. 3। শুকুৰবাৰ Friday.
entries.notes: 'ভৱগু' is DSAL OCR for ভৃগু. The dictionary has no entry for an evening-star word; that gap is recorded in summary_findings.

entries.literal_meaning: the wife of the sage Vasiṣṭha
entries.usage_note: Recorded here for its error, which is instructive. The Assamese definition is correct — Arundhatī is among the seven stars called the Saptarṣimaṇḍala, and Assamese brides are shown her at the wedding as the type of the faithful wife, and a person within six months of death cannot see her. The English gloss appended to it, 'the morning star; one of the pleiades', is wrong on both counts.
entries.citation: Candrakanta Abhidhana (Assamese-Assamese-English), 2nd ed., Guwahati: Guwahati Bisbabidyalaya for the Assam Sahitya Sabha, 1962 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. অৰুন্ধতী arundhatī, p. 48
entries.quote: …কৰ্দ্দম ঋষিৰ কন্যা আৰু বশিষ্ঠৰ ভাৰ্য্যা; [এওঁ সতী-ধৰ্ম্মত থকাৰ কাৰণে স্বামীৰে সৈতে স্বৰ্গৰ 'সপ্তৰ্ষিমণ্ডল বোলা তৰা সাতোটাৰ মাজত আছে বুলি ভবা হয়; হিন্দু ছোবালীক বিয়াৰ সময়ত এই নক্ষত্ৰক মহাসতী বুলি দেখুওবা ৰীতি আছে]; পৰমায়ু শেষ হ'লে অৰুন্ধতী দেখা নেপায় বুলি কয়; wife of the sage Vȧśiṣṭha; the morning star; one of the pleiades.
entries.notes: HOMONYM/ERROR WARNING. The English 'the morning star; one of the pleiades' contradicts the Assamese text of the same entry and every other source in this file. The Odia parallel is exact and correct: Praharaj (p. 570, and p. 54 s.v. ଅକ୍ଷମାଳା) makes Arundhatī the small star beside the 6th star of the Great Bear, i.e. Alcor, and preserves the Suśruta belief that one who will die within six months cannot see her. The Pleiades confusion has a traceable cause, given in Praharaj p. 4095: the other six ṛṣi-wives, unlike Arundhatī, were driven from their husbands' sides and became the Kṛttikās.

entries.sky_object: Venus as evening star (and, in the addenda, as morning star)
entries.literal_meaning: 'the big star' — the Assamese gloss opens বৰ তৰা, 'great star'
entries.usage_note: This fills the one gap the modern Assamese dictionary leaves: the Candrakanta Abhidhana has পুবঁতী তৰা for Venus as morning star but NO evening-star word at all. Bronson has both — the main entry gives the evening star, and the Addenda at the back of the volume add the morning star to the same headword.
entries.citation: M. Bronson, A Dictionary in Assamese and English, Sibsagor: American Baptist Mission Press, 1867, s.v. ভোটাতৰা, p. 439 (with Addenda, p. 608)
entries.quote: ভোটাতৰা, s. বৰ তৰা, চাইউঁৰিয়া সকত তৰা, a large star, Venus, the evening star.
entries.notes: Transcribed by me directly from the page image linked above; the archive.org OCR of Bronson's Assamese fount is unusable noise and cannot be relied on for any headword in this dictionary. The second Assamese word in the gloss, চাইউঁৰিয়া, is legible but its sense is not clear to me and I have not guessed at it. The folio number is the scan's pagination (leaf n450). The Addenda entry, reported in the same scan, reads 'ভোটাতৰা, s. add …, also the morning star' — i.e. Bronson corrected himself, reaching the same conclusion Praharaj states for Odia, that the two apparitions are one body.

entries.literal_meaning: 'tailed star' — Bronson's Assamese gloss spells it out, নেজ লগা তৰা, 'a star with a tail attached'
entries.usage_note: The 1867 attestation of the word the Candrakanta Abhidhana still carries in 1962 (p. 562), which makes it the best-dated vernacular star-word in this file. Bronson's neighbouring entries give the Assamese meteor vocabulary too: উল্কাপাত at p. 72 is glossed with পপিয়া তৰা, and ধুমকেতু at p. 308 is glossed as a meteor rather than a comet.
entries.citation: M. Bronson, A Dictionary in Assamese and English, Sibsagor: American Baptist Mission Press, 1867, s.v. নেজাল তৰা, p. 327
entries.quote: নেজাল তৰা, s. নেজ লগা তৰা বিসেস, a comet.
entries.notes: Graded likely, not certain, on a point of method: unlike the ভোটাতৰা entry I did not myself read this page image, and Bronson's Assamese cannot be checked against the OCR. The English gloss 'a comet' is confirmed present in the OCR at the corresponding point, and the Assamese form agrees exactly with the Candrakanta Abhidhana's নেজাল তৰা (p. 562). Also note Bronson p. 72, where the Assamese vernacular for a meteor is পপিয়া তৰা — the same word the Candrakanta prints as পপীয়া তৰা.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the man of Kāla / Death' — Praharaj's gloss makes the body black: 'the black bodied hideous messenger of the God of Death'
entries.usage_note: The Odia entry is the one that preserves the colour term the Bengali dictionary drops, and it also anatomises the figure: head = Mṛgaśirā, one shoulder = Ārdrā, waist-belt = the three stars Ilwaḻā; another name Agrahāyaṇī.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. କାଳପୁରୁଷ Kāḻapurusha, p. 1552
entries.quote: କାଳପୁରୁଷ— Kāḻapurusha ସଂ. ବି— 1। କୃଷ୍ଣବର୍ଣ୍ଣ ଶରୀରବିଶିଷ୍ଟ ବିକଟାକାର ଯମଙ୍କ କିଙ୍କର… — 1. The black bodied hideous messenger of the God of Death who comes to dying people with J̄ama's order to take them. 2। ଯମ—2. The God of Death. 3। ପୁରୁଷାକୃତ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ରପୁଞ୍ଜ— 3. The constellation Orion. [ଦ୍ର—ଏହାର ମସ୍ତକ ମୃଗଶିରା ଓ ଗୋଟିଏ ଖୁଆମୁଣ୍ଡି ଆର୍ଦ୍ରା; ଏହାର କଟିବନ୍ଧ ଇଲ୍ୱଳା ତାରକାତ୍ରୟ। ଏହାର ଅନ୍ଯ ନାମ ଅଗ୍ରହାୟଣୀ।]
entries.notes: Praharaj marks the headword ସଂ. (Sanskrit) — that is a statement about the morphemes, not about the constellation sense, which is sense 3 and has no Sanskrit precedent. Sense 4 is the jyotiṣa 'zodiacal man', the genuinely Sanskrit meaning, and Praharaj keeps the two apart.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the Ārdrā-row' — the string of stars containing Ārdrā
entries.usage_note: Marked ଗ୍ରା. (grāmya, rustic). The variants ଆର୍ଦ୍ରାବଳି Ārdrābaḻi (p. 814, marked ଦେ. deśī, sense 4 'The constellation of orion') and ଅରାବଳି Arābaḻī (p. 564, ଦେ. 'ଆର୍ଦ୍ରାବଳି; କାଳପୁରୁଷ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ରପୁଞ୍ଜ — The constellation of Orion') give the same word at three degrees of erosion.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ଅଦ୍ରାବଳି Adrābaḻi, p. 236
entries.quote: ଅଦ୍ରାବଳି— Adrābaḻi ଗ୍ରା. ବି. (ସଂ. ଆର୍ଦ୍ରା)— … 3। (ସଂ. ଆର୍ଦ୍ରା+ଆବଳି)—ଆର୍ଦ୍ରାନକ୍ଷତ୍ର ସମନ୍ୱିତ କାଳପୁରୁଷ ନାମକ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର ପୁଞ୍ଜ — 3. The constellation of Orion. ପୂର୍ବେ ଅଦ୍ରାବଳୀ ପଶ୍ଚିମେ ରୋଇ / ନାଥ ବୋଲେ ପୁତାରେ ନିଶ୍ଚେ ଯିବ ଧୋଇ। ଡାକବଚନ।
entries.notes: CAUTION ON THE PROVERB. The Ḍākabacana couplet appended here ('Adrābaḻī in the east, Roi in the west — Nātha says, my son, it will surely be washed away') is printed by Praharaj under THREE different headwords, and under two of them the word means a RAINBOW, not Orion: ଆର୍ଦାବଳି p. 813 (ଗ୍ରା., 'ଇନ୍ଦ୍ରଧନୁ — Rainbow') and ଆର୍ଦ୍ରାବଳି p. 814 sense 1 ('Rainbow'), and ରୋଇ is itself a straight rainbow (see ଋଜୁରୋହିତ p. 1080). The couplet is therefore a rain-prognostic about rainbows east and west; it is NOT evidence that Orion was an agricultural marker. I record it because Praharaj attached it to the Orion sense, and I flag the attachment as wrong.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the yoked plough' — naṅgal is the western-Odia form of laṅgaḻa, a plough
entries.usage_note: THE agricultural entry in this file. Praharaj's note: the Khaṛiās of Sambalpur do not yoke the plough — that is, do not begin the paddy sowing — until this asterism has risen, which is to say not before the month of Baiśākha; and it is for that reason that the cluster is called Naṅgal-juṛā.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ନଙ୍ଗଲ ଜୁଡ଼ା Naṅgal juṟḍ̠ā, p. 4106
entries.quote: ନଙ୍ଗଲ ଜୁଡ଼ା— Naṅgal juṟḍ̠ā ପ୍ରାଦେ. (ସମ୍ବଲପୁର) ବି— ତାରାପୁଞ୍ଜବିଶେଷ; ଇଲ୍ୱଳା ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର (କାଳପୁରୁଷର କଟିବନ୍ଧନ)— The belt of Orion (a constellation). [ଦ୍ର—ସମ୍ବଲପୁରର ଖଡ଼ିଆମାନେ ଏ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ରର ଉଦୟ ନ ହେଲେ (ବୈଶାଖ ମାସ ନ ହେଲେ) ଲଙ୍ଗଳ ଯୋଚନ୍ତି ନାହିଁ ଅର୍ଥାତ୍ ଧାନବୁଣାବୁଣି କାମ କରନ୍ତି ନାହିଁ । ଏଣୁ ଏ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର ପୁଞ୍ଜକୁ 'ନଙ୍ଗଲଜୁଡ଼ା' ବୋଲାଯାଏ ।]
entries.notes: Register tagged folk rather than tribal: the WORD is marked ପ୍ରାଦେ. (ସମ୍ବଲପୁର), i.e. provincial western Odia, and it is the OBSERVANCE that Praharaj attributes to the Khaṛiā (ଖଡ଼ିଆ) community. Astronomically the note is loose — Orion's Belt is a winter object and is already setting in the evening by Baiśākha (April-May); the practical marker is presumably the belt's heliacal or seasonal disappearance rather than a rising, or the 'rising' is a morning one. I have not emended Praharaj.

entries.literal_meaning: Ilvala, the asura brother of Vātāpi killed by Agastya
entries.usage_note: Praharaj supports it with a line of Rādhānātha Rāya's Yayāti: 'these three forms appear in one line, like Ilwaḻā in the sky'.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ଇଲ୍ୱଳା Ilwaḻā, p. 876
entries.quote: ଇଲ୍ୱଳା— Ilwaḻā ସଂ. ବି— କାଳପୁରୁଷ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ରପୁଞ୍ଜର କଟିଦେଶରେ ଥିବା ତିନିଟି ତାରା The Orion's belt. (ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର ତଳେ ନୋଟ ଦେଖ) ଏ ତିନିମୂର୍ତ୍ତି ଏକ ରେଖାରେ ଦିଶଇ ଇଳ୍ୱଳା ଯଥା ଆକାଶେ। —ରାଧାନାଥ, ଯଯାତି।
entries.notes: Sanskrit Ilvalāḥ is a name of the stars of Orion's HEAD (see sanskrit database id ilvala, from the Taittirīya tradition); Odia has moved the name down the figure to the BELT. That shift is worth recording: the two databases hold the same word against two different asterisms, and the Odia use is consistent across Praharaj (here, at ନଙ୍ଗଲ ଜୁଡ଼ା p. 4106, and at କାଳପୁରୁଷ p. 1552).

entries.sky_object: Orion's Belt (the three stars, individually named)
entries.literal_meaning: Uṣā daughter of king Bāṇa, her husband Aniruddha, and her companion Citralekhā
entries.usage_note: From Praharaj's long systematic note on the Kālapuruṣa group (item 36 under the headword ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର), which numbers 21 stars of Orion and gives each a name. Stars 6, 7, 8 are Uṣā, Aniruddha and Citralekhā individually and 'ଇଷୁ ତ୍ରିକାଣ୍ଡ ବା ପାଶୁପତ ବାଣ' (the three-jointed arrow, or the Pāśupata shaft) collectively.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର Nakshatra, note item 36 କାଳପୁରୁଷ ପୁଞ୍ଜ, p. 4095
entries.quote: 5 କାର୍ତ୍ତିକେୟ, 6 ଉଷା, 7 ଅନିରୁଦ୍ଧ 8 ଚିତ୍ରଲେଖା; 6। 7। 8 ଇଷୁ ତ୍ରିକାଣ୍ଡ ବା ପାଶୁପତ ବାଣ, 9। 10।11।12।13 ମୟୂରତୁଣ୍ଡ, 14 କାର୍ତ୍ତବୀର୍ଯ୍ୟ 15 ବାଣରାଜ 16 ଠାରୁ 21 କାଳପୁରୁଷର ଧନୁ। … —English Orion; 1, 2, 3, Orion's head, 4 Betelgeux, 5 Bellatrix, 6 Al Nitak, 7 Al Nilam, 8 Mintaka 6.7.8 Orion's belt. 9. 10 11. 12. 13 Orion's dagger, 14 Saiph, 15 Rigel, 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. 21 Orion's bow.
entries.notes: The Uṣā-Aniruddha-Citralekhā naming of the three belt stars is not in the Sanskrit database and I have found it in no Sanskrit source; it belongs to the Odia astronomical tradition Praharaj is codifying. Bellatrix as Kārttikeya and Saiph as Kārtavīrya likewise.

modern_star.common_name: Orion's Sword / dagger, incl. the Orion Nebula

entries.usage_note: Stars 9-13 of Praharaj's Orion diagram, identified in the same entry as σ, 42, θ, ι and υ Orionis and as 'Orion's dagger'.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର Nakshatra, note item 36 କାଳପୁରୁଷ ପୁଞ୍ଜ, p. 4095
entries.notes: I have not traced Mayūratuṇḍa as a star-name in any Sanskrit text; it may be Praharaj's own tradition or his own coinage for the western 'dagger'. Graded likely for that reason. Rigel is ବାଣରାଜ Bāṇarāja 'king Bāṇa' in the same list — the father of Uṣā, so the whole southern half of the figure is read as the Uṣā-Aniruddha story.

modern_star.common_name: Meissa and the head of Orion

entries.usage_note: Praharaj counts five stars on the top of the figure where the Sanskrit sources count three.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ସୌମ୍ୟ Sa̲u̲mya, p. 8756
entries.quote: A name given to the 5 stars (in plural) situate on the top of the Orion constellation; the Orion's head.
entries.notes: Linked to the Sanskrit database entry saumya (= Meissa / Mṛgaśīrṣa). The feminine ସୌମ୍ୟା at the same page is glossed 'The Orion's head (constellation)'. The count of five rather than three is Praharaj's.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the mallet star' — Praharaj glosses kaṭhalā in this phrase as ବଢ଼େଇର ମୁଗୁର, the carpenter's mallet
entries.usage_note: Given as the Sambalpuri name in Praharaj's systematic note on Kṛttikā, immediately after the general Odia name. The shape is argued for in the same entry: joining the six stars gives 'the shape of a dagger, or of a carpenter's wooden mallet'.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର Nakshatra, note on the 3rd asterism କୃତ୍ତିକା, p. 4095
entries.quote: ଆକାର ଓ ତାରକା ସଂଖ୍ୟା—6 ଟି ତାରା; ଏମାନଙ୍କୁ ଯୋଗ କଲେ ଗୋଟିଏ କଟାର ବା ବଢ଼େଇର କାଠମୁଗୁରାର ଆକାର ହେବ … ଓଡ଼ିଆ ବା ଦେଶୀୟନାମ—କାର୍ତ୍ତିକପୁଞ୍ଜା; ସମ୍ବଲପୁରୀ ନାମ କଠଲା ତାରା (କଠଲା=ବଢ଼େଇର ମୁଗୁର)। ପାଶ୍ଚାତ୍ୟ ନାମ—ଇଂ—Hen and chickens; the Pleides.
entries.notes: Praharaj's own headword କଠଲା (p. 1245) gives a different sense — a railed wooden seat strapped on an elephant — and does not record 'mallet'. The mallet gloss exists only here, inside the parenthesis, and is presumably the Sambalpuri sense. Worth flagging: a reader working from the headword alone would misread the star-name as 'the howdah-seat star'.

entries.usage_note: Marked ଦେ. (deśī), i.e. a native formation, not a tatsama: Odia has built its own compound on Kṛttikā rather than borrowing the Sanskrit name outright. Praharaj illustrates it with a ḍhaga (proverb): 'you pointed out the Kārttika cluster and I pointed out a gourd; whatever thief has got into my house, let him go out in front of me.'
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. କାର୍ତ୍ତିକପୁଞ୍ଜ Kārttikapun̄ja, p. 1538
entries.quote: କାର୍ତ୍ତିକପୁଞ୍ଜ— Kārttikapun̄ja ଦେ. ବି—(ସଂ. କୃତ୍ତିକା ଓ ପୁଞ୍ଜ) କୃତ୍ତିକା ନକ୍ଷତ୍ରପୁଞ୍ଜ— The constellation of the Pleiades. ତୁ ଦେଖାଇଲୁ କାର୍ତ୍ତିକ ପୁଞ୍ଜା ମୁଁ ଦେଖେଇଲି ଲାଉ; ମୋ ଘରେ ଯେଉଁ ଚୋର ପଶିଛି ସେ ମୋହରି ଆଗରେ ଯାଉ। ଢଗ।

entries.usage_note: Given as THE Odia or native name of the group in Praharaj's systematic note, against Hindi ଖଟୋଲା khaṭolā (a cot). The seven ṛṣis have become seven brothers.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର Nakshatra, note item 29 ସପ୍ତର୍ଷିମଣ୍ଡଳ, p. 4095
entries.quote: ଆକାର ଓ ତାରକା ସଂଖ୍ୟା—ଏ ତାରା 7ଟିକୁ ଯୋଗ କଲେ ଗୋଟିଏ ବେଣ୍ଟଲଗା କରଚୂଲି ପରି ହେବ। ଓଡ଼ିଆ ବା ଦେଶୀୟ ନାମ—ଓଡ଼ିଆ ସାତଭାଇୟା, ହିନ୍ଦି, ଖଟୋଲା। ପାଶ୍ଚାତ୍ୟ ନାମ—The Great Bear; the plough; charle's wain; the waggon; the Butcher's cleaver;
entries.notes: The shape metaphor in the same sentence is Odia too: joining the seven gives 'a karacūli with a handle', a long-handled ladle or scoop — independently the same idea as the English Dipper.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the bier' — the bamboo bedstead on which a corpse is carried to the burning-ground
entries.usage_note: Sense 1 of the same headword is the object itself. The Big Dipper as a bier is a real folk figure and reads the asterism the way Hindi khaṭolā and Arabic na'sh do — as a funeral cot, the four bowl stars the frame and the three handle stars the mourners.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ବାଜ୍ଖଟ୍ Bāj-khaṭ, p. 5484
entries.quote: ବାଜ୍ଖଟ୍— Bāj-khaṭ ପ୍ରାଦେ. (ସମ୍ବଲପୁର) ବି— 1। ମୁର୍ଦାର ବୁହା ଖଟିଆ; କୋକେଇ—1. A bamboo bedstead or stretcher for carrying a corpse. 2। ସପ୍ତର୍ଷିମଣ୍ଡଳ (ତାରାପୁଞ୍ଜ)—2. The Great Bear (group of stars).
entries.notes: The bier reading is my gloss on the two senses standing in one entry; Praharaj does not spell out the connection. The parallel with Hindi khaṭolā 'small cot', which Praharaj himself cites for the same group at p. 4095, supports it.

modern_star.common_name: the Great Bear, in its use as the Pointers to Polaris

entries.literal_meaning: 'the Dhruva-shower', that which points out the pole star
entries.usage_note: A functional name, and one the same dictionary explains: extend the line joining the two stars at the head of the group and it passes beside Dhruvatārā. Sense 2 of the same word is the mariner's compass.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ଧ୍ରୁବ ଦର୍ଶକ Dhruba darṡaka, p. 4069
entries.quote: ଧ୍ରୁବ ଦର୍ଶକ— Dhruba darṡaka ସଂ. ବି— 1। ସପ୍ତର୍ଷିମଣ୍ଡଳ —1. The constellation of the Ursa Major; the Great Bear. [ଦ୍ର—ଏହି ମଣ୍ଡଳର ମୁଣ୍ଡରେ ଥିବା ଦୁଇ ତାରାର ସଂଯୋଜକ ରେଖାକୁ ବଢ଼ାଇଲେ ତାହା ଧ୍ରୁବତାରା ପାଖ ଦେଇ ଯାଏ।] 2। ଜାହାଜିଆମାନଙ୍କର ଦିଗ୍ବାରଣ ଯନ୍ତ୍ର— 2. The mariner's compass.
entries.notes: At p. 4095 Praharaj glosses the English term directly: 'ଏ ଦୁଇ ତାରାକୁ The Pointers (ଧ୍ରୁବତାରାର ପ୍ରଦର୍ଶକ ବା ଧ୍ରୁବଦର୍ଶକ) ବୋଲାଯାଏ' — so the word may be a calque on the English Pointers rather than an inherited name.

entries.usage_note: A second name for Arundhatī, and Praharaj gives the reason: the Saptarṣimaṇḍala encircles her like a rosary.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ଅକ୍ଷମାଳା Akshamāḻā, p. 54
entries.quote: 3। ବଶିଷ୍ଠପତ୍ନୀ ଅରୁନ୍ଧତୀ —3. A name of the wife of sage Baṡishṭha. 4। ସପ୍ତର୍ଷିମଣ୍ଡଳର ପୁଚ୍ଛସ୍ଥ ମଧ୍ୟ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର ବା 6ଷ୍ଠୀ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର ପାଖରେ ଥିବା କ୍ଷୁଦ୍ର ତାରକା —4. Alcor; the small star near the 6th star of the constellation, Great Bear. [ଦ୍ର—ସପ୍ତର୍ଷିମଣ୍ଡଳ ଅରୁନ୍ଧତୀ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ରକୁ ମାଳାକାରରେ ବେଢ଼ିଥିବାରୁ ଅରୁନ୍ଧତୀର ଏହି ନାମ।]

entries.literal_meaning: 'the elephant-road' — the trampled lane elephants drive through jungle
entries.usage_note: Given by Praharaj as THE Odia name of the galaxy, in square brackets after the Sanskrit, Latin and Greek names, at the end of his article on the Chāyāpatha. The literal sense is described in detail under the headword ହାତି (p. 9088): these lanes run for hundreds of kos, about twenty feet wide and twenty feet high, so cleanly stripped that they look swept.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର Nakshatra, note item 63 ଛାୟା ପଥ, p. 4095
entries.quote: ସଂ. ନାମ—ସୋମଧାରା, ଦେବପଥ, ନଭଃସରିତ୍, ଆକାଶ ଗଙ୍ଗା, ହରିତାଳୀ। ଇଂ. ନାମ—The milky way; galaxy. ଲାଟିନ୍—Via Lactea. ଗ୍ରୀକ୍—Galaxis. [ଓଡ଼ିଆନାମ—ହାତିଦଣ୍ଡା ]
entries.notes: The exact counterpart of Assamese হাতীপটি hātīpaṭi (this file). Two dictionaries compiled independently in Cuttack and Gauhati record the same jungle metaphor for the galaxy in two languages — good evidence that it is a genuine eastern-Indian folk name and not a lexicographer's invention.

entries.usage_note: The Sambalpuri form of the same name, entered twice with the same two senses in the same order — jungle elephant-track, then the galaxy.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ହାଁଥିଧରସା Hāñthi dharasā, p. 9036
entries.quote: ହାଁଥିଧରସା— Hāñthi dharasā ପ୍ରାଦେ (ସମ୍ବଲପୁର) ବି— 1। ହାତୀଦଣ୍ଡା; ଜଙ୍ଗଲରେ ହାତୀମାନଙ୍କ ପଥ—1. Elephant-track in jungles. 2। ଛୟାପଥ—2. The milky way.
entries.notes: Duplicated at p. 9096 as ହାଥି ଧର୍ସା Hāti dhar-sā, same marking, same two senses. 'ଛୟାପଥ' at p. 9036 is a misprint for ଛାୟାପଥ.

entries.literal_meaning: uncertain; the word's other senses are the Bhādra festival day and the sharp edge of a sword
entries.usage_note: Notable for its orientation clause, which none of the other Milky Way words in this file carry: the galaxy AS IT RUNS FROM SOUTH TO NORTH ACROSS THE SKY. Praharaj lists Haritāḻī among the Sanskrit names of the Chāyāpatha at p. 4095.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ହରିତାଳୀ Haritāḻī, p. 8973
entries.quote: The milky way in the sky extending north to south. 3। ଭାଦ୍ର ଶୁକ୍ଳ ଚତୁର୍ଥୀ (ମତାନ୍ତରରେ ଶୁକ୍ଳତୃତୀୟା)—3. The 4th day of the bright fortnight of Bhādra (or, according to some, the 3rd day.
entries.notes: Praharaj's three entries disagree with each other on direction: ହରିତାଳିକା p. 8972 and ହରିତାଲିକା p. 8973 both say 'extending from the south to the north', ହରିତାଳୀ p. 8973 says 'north to south'. Same thing, said twice, carelessly. I have not found the word as a Milky Way name in any Sanskrit lexicon, so the 'ସଂ. ନାମ' label at p. 4095 should be treated with reserve — hence sanskrit_db_id null.

entries.literal_meaning: uncertain; Praharaj marks it ସଂ. and offers no derivation
entries.usage_note: Praharaj identifies it flatly with Lubdhaka and with α Canis Majoris, and uses it as a fixed point elsewhere — Canopus is located 'in the southern sky, south of Praśwā' (p. 4095).
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ପ୍ରଶ୍ୱା Praṡwā, p. 5131
entries.quote: ପ୍ରଶ୍ୱା— Praṡwā ସଂ. ବି.— ପୁନର୍ବସୁ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର ପୁଞ୍ଜର ଉଜ୍ଜ୍ୱଳତମ ତାରା, ଏହାର ଅନ୍ୟ ନାମ ଲୁବ୍ଧକ (ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର ତଳେ ନୋଟ ଦେଖ)— The Dogstar; sirius; Alpha Canis Majoris.
entries.notes: Graded likely because of an internal problem: Praharaj calls Praśwā 'the brightest star of the Punarvasu group', and his Punarvasu diagram at p. 4095 is a six-star bow running from Castor and Pollux through Procyon to Sirius — i.e. he has stretched Punarvasu across three modern constellations. The identification with Sirius is nevertheless explicit and repeated. The word does not appear in the Sanskrit database and I have not traced it to a Sanskrit source.

entries.usage_note: The seasonal function is the whole point of the Odia entry: the star rises in śarat, and because river water clears in śarat, Hindus take the rising of Agasti to be the CAUSE of the clearing. The companion entry ଅଗସ୍ତ୍ୟୋଦୟ (p. 75) dates it to the 7th of Bhādra and glosses it as the beginning of Indian autumn.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ଅଗସ୍ତି Agasti, p. 74
entries.quote: 2। ଦକ୍ଷିଣାକାଶର ଉଜ୍ଜଳ ନକ୍ଷତ୍ରବିଶେଷ— A bright star in the southern sky; Canopus; Argus Alpha; Argo Navis. [ଦ୍ର—ଏହା ଶରତ୍କାଳରେ ଉଦିତ ହୁଏ; ଶରତ୍କାଳରେ ନଦ୍ୟାଦିର ଜଳ ନିର୍ମଳ ହେବାରୁ ଅଗସ୍ତି ନକ୍ଷତ୍ରର ଉଦୟକୁ ଜଳର ନିର୍ମଳତାର କାରଣ ବୋଲି ହିନ୍ଦୁମାନେ ବିଶ୍ୱାସ କରନ୍ତି।]
entries.notes: Praharaj adds at p. 4095 that Canopus was the southern pole star 14,000 years ago — a precession calculation, and a sign that this dictionary is drawing on European positional astronomy as well as on jyotiṣa.

entries.sky_object: a small star south-east of Canopus
entries.literal_meaning: Lopāmudrā, wife of the sage Agastya
entries.usage_note: Recorded twice: as a headword, and in the Canopus note at p. 4095 ('the small star to its south-east is Agastya's wife Lopāmudrā').
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ଲୋପା ମୁଦ୍ରା Lopā mudrā, p. 7452
entries.quote: 2। ଅଗସ୍ତି ନାମକ ତାରାର ଦକ୍ଷିଣ ପୂର୍ବ ପାଖରେ ଅବସ୍ଥିତ ଏକ କ୍ଷୁଦ୍ର ତାରା (ହି. ଶ.) (ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର ତଳେ ନୋଟ ଦେଖ) —2. A small star to the south east of Canopus (star).
entries.notes: DELIBERATELY LEFT UNIDENTIFIED. No candidate is named and 'small star south-east of Canopus' does not resolve: the plausible naked-eye options in that direction are several. sanskrit_db_id is null on purpose — the Sanskrit database's lopamudravallabha is 'Lopāmudrā's beloved', i.e. Agastya, i.e. CANOPUS ITSELF, a different star from this one. Recording them as the same entry would be an error. Praharaj credits the sense to the Hindī Śabdasāgara (ହି. ଶ.), so it may not be independently Odia.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the tale-telling star', from khaca, an account or report
entries.usage_note: The best piece of sky-lore in Praharaj. Because the star is seen sometimes before dawn and sometimes for a watch after nightfall, people believe it goes ahead to Yama and reports the doings of the people of this world.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ଖଚୁଆ ତରା Khachuā tarā, p. 1890
entries.quote: ଖଚୁଆ ତରା— Khachuā tarā ଦେ. ବି— ପାହାନ୍ତିଆ ତାରା— Morning Star. [ଦ୍ର—ଏ ତାରା କେତେକ ମାସ ରାତି ନ ପାହୁଣୁ ଓ କେତେକ ମାସ ରାତି ପହରକ ପର୍ଯ୍ୟନ୍ତ ଦେଖାଯିବାରୁ ଲୋକ ବିଶ୍ୱାସ ଯେ ଏ ପୃଥିବୀର ଲୋକଙ୍କ ନାମରେ ଯମ ଆଗରେ ଯାଇ ଖଚ କହେ।]
entries.notes: Note what the folk belief is doing: it is an explanation of Venus's alternation between morning and evening apparitions — the star is absent because it has gone to Yama's court to file its report. The literal meaning given here is my reading of khaca 'account, report' as used in the note itself.

entries.usage_note: Marked ପ୍ରାଦେ. (ଗଡ଼ଜାତ), provincial to the Garjat states. Defined by the clock and by the work it starts: the star that rises at 4 a.m., with the example sentence 'when Phukiā rises the fisherwomen begin husking chuṛā (flattened rice)'.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ଫୁକିଆ Phukiā, p. 5239
entries.quote: ଫୁକିଆ— Phukiā (ଫୁକିଆତରା—ଅନ୍ୟରୂପ) ପ୍ରାଦେ. (ଗଡ଼ଜାତ) ବି— ରାତି 4 ଟା ବେଳେ ଉଦିତ ହେବ ପାହାନ୍ତିଆ ତାରା; ଶୁକ୍ର ଗ୍ରହ— Morning star; the planet Venus rising in the early morning. (ଯଥା—ଫୁକିଆ ଉଠିଲେ କେଉଟୁଣିମାନେ ଚୁଡ଼ାକୁଟା ଆରମ୍ଭ କରନ୍ତି।)
entries.notes: A working-day marker rather than an agricultural-calendar marker: the star tells the hour, not the season. Paired with ଫୁକିଆ, note that the Sambalpuri name for the EVENING star is also a fisher word — କେଉଁଟି ତାରା, from keuṭa, the fisher caste.

entries.literal_meaning: a worn-down form of kāvya-tārā, 'the star of Kāvya' — Kāvya/Uśanas being Śukra, the preceptor of the asuras
entries.usage_note: Marked ଦେ., with the Sanskrit etymon given. Defined by the watch: the bright body that rises in the east with one prahara of night still to go.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. କୁଆତରା Kuātarā, p. 1613
entries.quote: କୁଆତରା— Kuātarā ଦେ. ବି. (ସଂ. କାବ୍ୟତାରା)— ପ୍ରଭାତ ହେବା ପୂର୍ବରୁ ରାତ୍ରି ଏକ ପ୍ରହର ଥାଇ ଯେଉଁ ଉଜ୍ଜ୍ୱଳ ଜ୍ୟୋତିଷ୍କ ପୂର୍ବଦିଗରେ ଉଦିତ ହୁଏ; ଶୁକ୍ରଗ୍ରହ—The morning star; Venus.
entries.notes: The tatsama it descends from is also in the dictionary: କାବ୍ୟତାରକା Kābytārakā, p. 1511, 'The morning star; Venus'. Odia thus has the same word twice, once learned and once worn down.

entries.usage_note: The general Odia term, and the one Praharaj uses to define all the others. His note is unusually careful: the morning star is NOT one body — at different times of year Mars, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn rise before dawn in the east, but Venus is the brightest of them and Jupiter next.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ପାହାନ୍ତି ତାରା Pāhānti tārā, p. 4814
entries.quote: The morning star; the shining star seen in the eastern sky before dawn. [ଦ୍ର—ଏହା ଗୋଟିଏ ନୁହେଁ, ବର୍ଷର ଭିନ୍ନ ଭିନ୍ନ ସମୟରେ ଭିନ୍ନ ଭିନ୍ନ ଗ୍ରହ ଯଥା—ମଙ୍ଗଳ, ବୃହସ୍ପତି, ଶୁକ୍ର ଓ ଶନି ପାହାନ୍ତିଆ ସମୟରେ ପୂର୍ବଦିଗରୁ ଉଅଁନ୍ତି—କିନ୍ତୁ ସମସ୍ତଙ୍କ ମଧ୍ୟରେ ଶୁକ୍ର ଉଜ୍ଜ୍ୱଳତମ ଓ ତା ପରେ ବୃହସ୍ପତି।]
entries.notes: This is the correct lexicographic position and it is worth flagging against the rest of this group: 'morning star' in Odia is a functional description, and only usually Venus. The doublet ପୁଆଁ ତରା Puāñ tarā (p. 4877, ଦେ., from ପ୍ରଭାତୀ ତାରା) is the worn-down form.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the fisherwoman's star' — keuṭa/keuṇṭa is the fisher caste
entries.usage_note: A caste-and-labour name for a planet: the star that goes down in the west a watch into the night, which Praharaj identifies flatly as Venus.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. କେଉଁଟି ତାରା Keuñṭi tārā, p. 1740
entries.quote: କେଉଁଟି ତାରା— Keuñṭi tārā ପ୍ରାଦେ. (ସମ୍ବଲପୁର) ବି— ପହରିକିଆ ତାରା; ପଶ୍ଚିମାକାଶରେ ରାତି ପହରକଠାରେ ବୁଡ଼ିବା ଜ୍ୟୋତିଷ୍କ (ଏହାହିଁ ଶୁକ୍ର ଅଟେ।)—Evening Star.
entries.notes: The 'fisherwoman' reading of keuñṭi is mine, from the caste name; Praharaj does not gloss it. It pairs with ଫୁକିଆ at p. 5239, whose example sentence is also about fisherwomen — so in western and princely Odisha both apparitions of Venus are named from the fishing household's working day.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the one-watch star' — the star that lasts a prahara
entries.usage_note: The general Odia evening-star word. Praharaj's note insists that it is not a star at all but a planet, and the same body as the morning star.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ପହରିକିଆ ତାରା Paharikiā tārā, p. 4687
entries.quote: ପହରିକିଆ ତାରା— Paharikiā tārā … ଦେ. ବି— ରାତି ପ୍ରହରକଠାରେ ପଶ୍ଚିମରେ ବୁଡ଼ିଯିବା ଶୁକ୍ର ଗ୍ରହ… —The Evening star; the Hesperus; Venus. [ଦ୍ର—ଏହି ପହରିକିଆ ତାରା ପ୍ରକୃତରେ ତାରା ନୁହେଁ; ଏହା ଗୋଟିଏ ଗ୍ରହ ଓ ଏହା ପୁଣି ପାହାନ୍ତି ତରା ରୂପେ କେତେଦିନ ପାହାନ୍ତିଆରେ ପୂର୍ବ ଦିଗରେ ଦେଖାଯାଏ।]
entries.notes: Praharaj's synonym column prints the Bengali equivalent of this Odia evening-star headword as শুকতারা (OCR'd on DSAL as 'ত্তকতারা'), and prints the same Bengali word against the MORNING-star headword ପୁଆଁ ତରା at p. 4877 (OCR'd 'গুকতারা'). That is direct cross-language evidence for the Bengali morning/evening ambiguity flagged in the শুকতারা entry.

entries.literal_meaning: 'tail-star'; Praharaj adds the reason — 'because it has a line of light in it like a tail'
entries.usage_note: Marked ଦେ. and illustrated from Rādhānātha Rāya's Yayāti. Variants and near-synonyms fill the same semantic field: ରଞ୍ଜା ତରା Rañjā tarā (p. 6955), ଲାଙ୍ଗୁଡ଼ା ତାରା Lāṅguṛā tārā (p. 7342), ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର ଲଞ୍ଜା Nakshatra lañjā (p. 4096), and ଲଞ୍ଜା alone (p. 7277).
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ଲଞ୍ଜା ତାରା Lan̄jā tārā, p. 7277
entries.quote: ଲଞ୍ଜା ତାରା— Lan̄jā tārā ଦେ. ବି — (ସଂ. ଲଞ୍ଜ+ତାରା)—(ଏଥିରେ ଲାଞ୍ଜ ପରି ଗୁଡ଼ିଏ ଆଲୋକ ରେଖା ଥିବାରୁ)— ଧୂମକେତୁ — Comet. [ଉ—ସ୍କନ୍ଧେ ମହାଶୂଳ ଲଞ୍ଜାତାରା କି ସେ ନାଶିବାକୁ ବୈରି କୁଳ। ରାଧାନାଥ. ଯଯାତି।]
entries.notes: The tail-star formation is pan-eastern: Assamese নেজাল তৰা nejāla tarā (this file), and Praharaj's own synonym column gives Bengali and Hindi cognates against the Odia headwords. The Bengali cognate is printed inconsistently in the DSAL transcription (লেজেতারা at one duplicate headword, নেজান তারা at the other), so I have not made a Bengali entry from it.

entries.sky_object: the Pole Star, and the south celestial pole

modern_star.common_name: Polaris; and, for ଯାମ୍ୟ ଧ୍ରୁବ, the south celestial pole

entries.usage_note: A pair coined to hold a fact European astronomy supplied: there are two poles, and only the northern one is visible from India. For the southern, Praharaj records the working substitute — since we cannot see it, the southernmost bright star of the Triśaṅku group above the south pole point is taken to be the south pole star.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ଯାମ୍ୟ ଧ୍ରୁବ J̄āmya dhruba, p. 6820
entries.quote: ଯାମ୍ୟ ଧ୍ରୁବ— J̄āmya dhruba … ବି— ଦକ୍ଷଣ ମେରୁ ଉପରେ ଥିବା ଧ୍ରୁବ ତାରା— The pole star on the south pole. [ଦ୍ର—ଏ ତାରାକୁ ଆମ୍ଭେମାନେ ଦେଖି ପାରୁ ନାହିଁ ବୋଲି ଦକ୍ଷିଣ ଧ୍ରୁବ ବିନ୍ଦୁର ଉପରକୁ ଥିବା ତ୍ରିଶଙ୍କୁ ମଣ୍ଡଳର ଦକ୍ଷିଣତମ ଉଜ୍ଜ୍ୱଳ ତାରାକୁ ଦକ୍ଷିଣ ଧ୍ରୁବ ତାରା ବୋଲି ଧରାଯାଏ।]
entries.notes: The Triśaṅku group is in the Sanskrit database (id trishanku) as the king fixed head-downward in the southern sky; Praharaj is using it as a real region of sky with a determinable southernmost member. ସୌମ୍ୟ ଧ୍ରୁବ is at p. 8756, ଧ୍ରୁବ ତାରା at p. 4068, ଉତ୍ତରଧ୍ରୁବ at p. 947.

modern_star.bayer: α, θ, γ, δ, ε Tauri

entries.usage_note: Given as the Odia or native name of the 4th asterism. The omen attached to it is recorded in the same note: when the moon is seen to pierce the Rohiṇī-cart, calamity is feared.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର Nakshatra, note on the 4th asterism ରୋହିଣୀ, p. 4095
entries.quote: 5 ଗୋଟି ତାରା, ଏ 5 ତାରାକୁ ଯୋଗକଲେ ଗୋଟିଏ ସମଦ୍ୱିବାହୁ ତ୍ରିଭୁଜ ବା ଶଗଡ଼ଦଣ୍ଡାର ଆକାର ହେବ। ଓଡ଼ିଆ ବା ଦେଶୀୟ ନାମ—ରୋହିଣୀ ଶକଟ। ପାଶ୍ଚାତ୍ୟ ନାମ—Hyades. … ଚନ୍ଦ୍ର ଯେବେ ରୋହିଣୀ— ଶକଟକୁ ଭେଦ କରିବାର ଦେଖାଯାଏ ତେବେ ଅନିଷ୍ଟ ଆଶଙ୍କା କରାଯାଏ।
entries.notes: The shape word ଶଗଡ଼ଦଣ୍ଡା śagaṛa-daṇḍā (the pole/shaft of a bullock cart) is Odia, and is what makes the Sanskrit śakaṭa figure legible to an Odia reader.

entries.usage_note: Given as the Odia or native name of Ārdrā — that is, the sixth nakṣatra is identified for an Odia reader not by a Sanskrit epithet but by its place on the Kālapuruṣa figure. The same note names Mṛgaśirā 'ଓଡ଼ିଆ ବା ଦେଶୀୟ ନାମ—କାଳପୁରୁଷର ମୁଣ୍ଡ', the head of Kālapuruṣa.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର Nakshatra, note on the 6th asterism ଆର୍ଦ୍ରା, p. 4095
entries.quote: ଆକାର ଓ ତାରକା ସଂଖ୍ୟା—ଗୋଟିଏ ହଳଦିଆ ଉଜ୍ଜ୍ୱଳ ତାରା। ଓଡ଼ିଆ ବା ଦେଶୀୟ ନାମ—କାଳପୁରୁଷର ଡାହାଣ ଖୁଆ ମୁଣ୍ଡ। ପାଶ୍ଚାତ୍ୟ ନାମ—Betelgeus.
entries.notes: This is the analytically important point about Odia: the Kālapuruṣa figure is not an ornament added on top of the nakṣatra system, it is the frame the nakṣatras of that part of the sky are described BY.

modern_star.bayer: λ Scorpii and the ε–υ chain

entries.usage_note: Given as the Odia or native name of the 19th asterism, whose eleven stars Praharaj describes as a pair of dogs. The Odia figure for the whole Scorpius region is spelled out in the Jyeṣṭhā note: joining the stars of Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā and Mūlā gives a crab-scorpion (କଙ୍କଡ଼ାବିଛା) with its tail curled up — head Anurādhā, back Jyeṣṭhā, tail Mūlā.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର Nakshatra, note on the 19th asterism ମୂଳା, p. 4095
entries.quote: 8 ଓ 9 ଚିହ୍ନିତ ତାରା ଦ୍ୱାରା ଯମଙ୍କର 2 ଟି କୁକୁର ବା ସାରମେୟ ଯୁଗଳ। ଓଡ଼ିଆ ବା ଦେଶୀୟ ନାମ—ମୂଳା ଶଙ୍ଖ। ପାଶ୍ଚାତ୍ୟ ନାମ—Scorpion's tail … ମନ୍ତବ୍ୟ—ଅନୁରାଧା, ଜ୍ୟେଷ୍ଠା ଓ ମୂଳା ନକ୍ଷତ୍ରର ତାରାମାନଙ୍କୁ କଳ୍ପନାଦ୍ୱାରା ଯୋଗ କଲେ ଲାଞ୍ଜକୁ ଉପରକୁ ଗୁଡ଼ାଇ କରି ଟେକିଥିବା ଗୋଟିଏ କଙ୍କଡ଼ାବିଛା ପରି ହେବ। ଏ ବିଛାର ମୁଣ୍ଡ ଅନୁରାଧା, ପିଠି ଜ୍ୟେଷ୍ଠା ଓ ଲାଙ୍ଗୁଡ଼ ମୂଳା।
entries.notes: Mūla's nine stars are λ (Shaula) and υ (Lesath) Scorpii and the chain ε, μ, ζ, η, θ, ι, κ, which Praharaj also reads as Yama's two dogs (stars 8 and 9). The Antares note in the same article identifies Jyeṣṭhā's three stars as σ, α (Antares) and τ Scorpii and calls Antares 'like a burning fire'; Antares itself has no separate Odia name in this dictionary.

entries.usage_note: Odia distinguishes the worn-down ତରା tarā, which is what all the folk compounds in this file are built on (khachuā tarā, phukiā tarā, keuñṭi tārā, lañjā tārā), from the tatsama ତାରକା tārakā, whose second sense is 'comet' — ଲଞ୍ଜା ତାରା.
entries.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-1940 (DSAL digital ed.), s.v. ତାରକା Tārakā, p. 3445
entries.quote: ସଂ. ବି. ସ୍ତ୍ରୀ (ତାରକ+ସ୍ତ୍ରୀ. ଆ)— 1। ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର— 1. Star. 2। ଲଞ୍ଜା ତାରା—2. Comet. 3। ଚକ୍ଷୁର ତାରା; କନୀନିକା— 3. The pupil of the eye.

caveats: SCOPE. This file holds Bengali, Assamese and Odia only. The Munda and Dravidian parallels that make the western-Odia folk layer intelligible — Santali arar 'the Yoke' for Orion's Belt, Mundari moṅgaru ipilko 'the wooden mallet' for the Pleiades and topaḍ parkom ipilko 'the bier stars' for the Big Dipper, Kurukh khaṭī pāwā bīnkō and ugtā pagsi bīnkō, the Mundari and Kurukh cattle-track names for the Milky Way — are documented in the notes of the Odia entries with author, page and edition, but are NOT entered here as records: they belong to the sibling file sources/tribal.json, which covers them in far more detail. One body of tribal material found in this pass appears NOT to be covered there and should be added to it rather than to this file: Sarat Chandra Roy, The Birhors (Ranchi, 1925), pp. 386 and 496, giving Birhor [biy] Bhurka for Venus as morning star, Kidu Ipil for the evening star, Kumbūru lagu Ipil 'thief-driving star' for a bright object rising before Bhurka, the famine forecast read from which of the two apparitions is the more prominent in a given year, and chāndi for a meteor, at which all Birhors spit.

COPYRIGHT. Praharaj (1931-40), Dāsa (1937), Haughton (1833), Ram Comul Sen (1834), Bronson (1867), Campbell (1899), Hahn (1903), Risley (1891) and Roy (1925) are out of copyright. Two are not: DSAL prints copyright notices for the Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed. (2000, Shishu Sahitya Samsad) and the Candrakanta Abhidhana, 2nd ed. (1962, Assam Sahitya Sabha), and the Encyclopaedia Mundarica's status was not established. What is quoted from those is in every case a single short lemma, quoted because a name without its printed definition is not citable evidence. Anyone republishing this database should re-examine that judgement.

OCR AND SCRIPT. Three separate transcription problems are flagged per entry rather than silently fixed. (1) The DSAL transcription of the Candrakanta Abhidhana renders the Assamese vowel sign ৃ as ৱ throughout — মৱত্যু for মৃত্যু, কৱত্তিকা for কৃত্তিকা, বৱষ for বৃষ. (2) The archive.org OCR of Hoffmann, Campbell and Roy mangles the roman diacritics (moT^garuipilko for moṅgaru ipilko, Bhtirka for Bhurka); these are quoted as scanned with the normalised reading marked editorial in the notes. (3) The archive.org OCR of Bengali, Assamese and Odia SCRIPT is unusable in every scanned book tried — Bronson, Carey, Morton, Sykes, Sutton, Ram Comul Sen. Where the script was needed it was read off the page image; where it could not be read, the entry was dropped rather than back-transliterated.

WHAT I READ MYSELF. Every DSAL quotation was fetched and its presence at its own source_url verified programmatically. Of the page-image sources I read three images directly — Haughton p. 419, Ram Comul Sen vol. 2 p. 168, Bronson p. 439. The remaining image-sourced material (Bronson p. 327, Hahn's Kurukh set, the Hoffmann passages taken from the scans rather than the OCR stream) was transcribed by a second reader working to the same rules; those entries are graded 'likely' rather than 'certain' and say so in their notes.

Praharaj duplicates many headwords under variant spellings (ଶୁକ୍ ତରା / ଶୁକ୍ ତାରା, ପହରିକିଆ ତରା / ପହରିକିଆ ତାରା, ହରିତାଳିକା / ହରିତାଲିକା / ହରିତାଳୀ) and the duplicates sometimes disagree — the three Haritāḻī entries cannot agree whether the Milky Way runs north to south or south to north. Where duplicates exist one has been made the entry and the others named in its notes. He also prints Bengali and Hindi equivalents in a synonym column; those are second-hand and their DSAL transcription is unreliable (the same Bengali word appears as লেজেতারা at one duplicate headword and নেজান তারা at the other), so no entry rests on them.

DSAL's headword index and the query URL are byte-sensitive: পপীয়া is indexed with the precomposed U+09DF and ଯାମ୍ୟ with U+0D5F, and a query typed with the nukta sequence returns nothing. DSAL's `page=N` browse also silently jumps to the start of an indexing block, so it is not a reliable citation target. Every source_url here is a headword or full-text query that was fetched and checked, except where a `page=` URL was verified to contain the quoted text.

REGISTER tags describe how the NAME is formed and where it is used, not the etymology of every morpheme. কালপুরুষ is 'vernacular' although both its parts are Sanskrit, because the application to Orion is an eastern New Indo-Aryan development. ନଙ୍ଗଲ ଜୁଡ଼ା is 'folk' rather than 'tribal' because Praharaj marks the WORD provincial Sambalpuri and attributes only the OBSERVANCE to the Khaṛiās. 'tribal' is reserved for names recorded in a tribal language.

LITERAL MEANINGS marked as the compiler's in the notes (kukurabāhī, keuñṭi, bāj-khaṭ as 'bier', khacuā) are readings of the compound, not the dictionaries'. Where a dictionary supplies the gloss itself — kaṭhalā = the carpenter's mallet, jhām̐ṭā = because it is shaped like a broom — that is stated.

sanskrit_db_id points at the entry in docs/star-names/star-names.json for the same SKY OBJECT, so the two databases can be joined on the object. It does not assert that the vernacular name descends from the Sanskrit one; the register field says that. It is null where no counterpart entry exists (Venus, comets, meteors) or where linking would assert a false identity — ଲୋପାମୁଦ୍ରା, a small star south-east of Canopus, is deliberately NOT linked to lopamudravallabha, which is Canopus itself.

NOT SEARCHED, and worth a later pass: the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, which is large and was not reached; Bodding's Santal Dictionary vols 1-4, which are not readily findable online and would almost certainly deepen the Santali set; Encyclopaedia Mundarica vols 1, 4 and 8, which carry cross-references to the Orion and Pleiades material that were not chased to printed pages; and Bengali-language popular astronomy and almanacs, which are effectively unsearchable because Bengali-script OCR yields no greppable text — they would have to be read page by page.

The register value 'tribal' is unused in this file by design - see the scope caveat. The registers present are sanskritic, vernacular and folk. 'folk' is applied only where the dictionary itself marks the word rustic or provincial: Praharaj's ଗ୍ରା. (gramya) and ପ୍ରାଦେ. (pradesika, with the district named - Sambalpur, Garjat), and Dāsa's গ্রা◦.
